From the owner
You pull a tray out of the oven and notice the white coating on the cabinet door next to it is curling away at the edge, with brown board showing underneath. Then you check the door on the other side and it's doing the same thing. That almost never means the cabinets are falling apart. Doors like these are thermofoil, which is a thin vinyl skin glued over fiberboard, and the glue lets go when it gets hot enough. That's why it starts beside the oven or over the toaster while the doors across the room look fine. The self-clean cycle is the usual trigger, and a lot of ovens get run through it this time of year ahead of Thanksgiving. The cabinet boxes behind those doors are usually in good shape, so the fix tends to be small. A corner that still lies flat can sometimes be glued back down. Once the film has shrunk or bubbled it won't go back, and the answer is new doors for those spots or stripping the film and painting. Before the next self-clean, take the doors on either side of the oven off their hinges. It only takes a few minutes. This recent bathroom remodel showcases how the right combination of materials can transform an everyday space into a private spa. One of the standout trends in modern design is the use of a double vanity featuring fluted wood textures, which brings natural warmth to the room and blends harmoniously with the bright quartz countertops and wall tiling. Beyond the wood textures, incorporating brass or gold finishes on the faucets and cabinet hardware adds a layer of refined elegance without overwhelming the eye. Because functionality is just as important as aesthetics in a bathroom remodel, proper lighting is absolutely critical. Pairing LED-backlit mirrors with upper wall sconces ensures an even, shadow-free distribution of light, significantly improving daily comfort and usability. As a premier general contractor in Redmond, Washington, Anyvision Home Remodeling believes that a successful bathroom renovation starts with meticulous planning—from the initial 3D design phase straight through to the final finishes. From the owner
This kitchen balances warmth, texture, and restraint — where every detail serves a purpose without drawing unnecessary attention to itself. The green tile backsplash became the defining element later in the design. It adds a sense of depth and tone variation, bringing life to the space while staying true to a mid-century palette. Its subtle gloss finish allows light to move across the surface, changing character throughout the day. To ground the color, we paired it with custom wood cabinetry. The natural grain introduces warmth and texture, a deliberate contrast to the cooler tile tones. Each panel was selected and aligned to maintain a continuous flow — a small detail, but one that gives the cabinetry its furniture-grade feel. Lighting was layered rather than centralized. Custom fixtures were chosen to emphasize surfaces, creating even illumination that defines the materials rather than flattening them. The result is a kitchen that feels both current and timeless — comfortable, functional, and built around human scale rather than trend. Built by Aurea Construction.

From the owner
Older homes in the Ellicott City area often share the same infrastructure surprises as DC's pre-1980 rowhouses: aluminum wiring, galvanized pipes, aging boilers, and occasionally knob-and-tube wiring or asbestos. Before framing a single wall, those systems typically need to be addressed - and that work runs $15,000-$40,000 on its own, separate from the finishing cost. If your project also requires basement lowering, that adds another $40,000-$200,000 depending on scope. Knowing these layers upfront is what separates a realistic budget from an unpleasant mid-project surprise. If you're planning a basement remodel in a historic or older home, it pays to get a full infrastructure assessment before you commit to a finish plan.

In Lakewood Ranch, kitchen design has taken on a more refined, elevated feel—where clean lines meet effortless functionality, and every detail is thoughtfully curated. At the heart of these beautiful spaces? Custom cabinetry that blends sophistication with everyday comfort. One of the most sought-after styles right now is European-inspired cabinetry. Known for its sleek, handleless profiles and minimalist elegance, this look creates a seamless, uncluttered aesthetic while maximizing storage in the most graceful way. Beyond that, homeowners are embracing features that feel both luxurious and practical: Full-height cabinetry that draws the eye upward and creates a grand, tailored appearance Integrated storage solutions like hidden drawers and pull-outs that keep everything beautifully organized and out of sight Layered materials and finishes that add richness, texture, and visual depth to the space What makes custom cabinetry truly special is the ability to personalize every element. From the finish to the function, each detail is designed to reflect your lifestyle—whether you love to entertain, cook, or simply enjoy a serene, polished environment. From the owner
An unfinished basement or awkward interior layout usually starts with the same question: should you move a wall, add one, or leave the structure alone? That is where a contractor’s planning matters before any visible work begins. In homes across Windsor, Fort Collins, Loveland, and nearby communities, we often see projects slow down because the framing, access, electrical paths, and future use of the space were not thought through early. A wall is not just a wall if it affects traffic flow, storage, door swing, lighting, or what sits behind it. A good contractor helps you look at the full picture first: how the space will function day to day, what needs to stay accessible, where clean transitions matter, and how to avoid changes mid-project that add cost and delay. That is especially important if you are converting underused square footage into a home office, guest area, playroom, or more practical family space. If you are considering an interior reconfiguration, start with a plan instead of a demo list. Clear scope and sequencing usually lead to a smoother project and a finished space that works better long after construction is done.

From the owner
Integrating modern storage solutions into the architecture of a century-old home requires a delicate balance of contemporary function and historic preservation. When designing a new layout for classic properties in Moorestown, Haddonfield, and Collingswood, off-the-shelf cabinetry rarely fits the unique proportions of the space. Older kitchens often feature oversized original windows, low-hanging structural soffits, and multiple architectural doorways that interrupt standard continuous wall runs. A successful design strategy embraces these historic quirks rather than fighting them. We utilize custom-sized upper cabinets to perfectly frame large antique windows, maximizing vertical storage without blocking precious natural light. Additionally, integrating specialized base units like deep pull-out drawers and corner blind organizers ensures you gain exceptional modern utility even if your floor plan is highly unconventional. Precise installation is equally critical; because classic homes have settled over the decades, every individual cabinet box must be meticulously scribed to fit tightly against uneven plaster walls and sloping hardwood floors. The result is a beautifully integrated kitchen that delivers state-of-the-art organization while honoring the timeless elegance of your historic residence. Call to discuss custom cabinetry design and layout for your classic home.

From the owner
Luxury vinyl plank flooring installed in a Bellevue living room, laid over a subfloor that was checked, dried and leveled before a single plank went down. That step is what keeps a floor from flexing underfoot or separating at the seams a year later, and it is the step most quotes quietly leave out. Here is what the job actually involved. The old flooring came up first, the substrate was checked for moisture and flat spots, and the low areas were leveled so the planks would sit tight across the whole room. Then underlayment, then the planks, then new baseboard and clean transitions at every doorway, so the floor reads as part of the house rather than something laid on top of it. LVP has become the default choice across the Eastside for good reasons. It is waterproof, it is quiet to walk on, it handles kids, pets and wet boots through a Washington winter, and it costs far less than hardwood while looking close to it. It is not the right answer for every room, though, and we will tell you honestly when hardwood or tile would serve your house better. We install flooring for homeowners in Bellevue, Kirkland, Redmond, Bothell, Sammamish, Issaquah and Woodinville. Six month workmanship warranty on everything we install. Free in home estimate, in English or Portuguese, Monday to Saturday.

How Long Does a Bathroom Remodel Take? One of the first questions homeowners ask is, “How long will my bathroom remodel take?” While every project is unique, most full bathroom remodels typically take 3 to 6 weeks once construction begins. The timeline can vary depending on: ✔ The size of the bathroom ✔ Material availability ✔ Custom cabinetry or specialty finishes ✔ Plumbing or electrical changes ✔ Permit and inspection requirements One of the best ways to keep a project on schedule is to make material selections before construction begins. Choosing fixtures, tile, cabinetry, and finishes early helps reduce delays and keeps the project moving smoothly. A well-planned remodel isn’t just about creating a beautiful space—it’s also about creating an efficient construction process.

Does your deck need replacing, or just resurfacing? Fall is the right time to look closely at your deck — before winter, and before next spring’s build season fills up. Here’s how to tell the difference. The cost gap between the two is substantial. Resurfacing may be enough if: The framing, posts, and footings are solid. You can push hard against the railing and nothing moves. No soft spots when you press a screwdriver into the joists or ledger board. The problem is surface-level — splintering boards, failed stain, cupping or cracking decking. New decking and railing over sound framing costs meaningfully less than a full rebuild. Full replacement is the answer if: The ledger board — where the deck attaches to your house — shows rot or inadequate flashing. This is the most common point of deck failure. Posts are rotted at the base or set directly in soil without proper footings. The structure sways when you walk on it. Joist hangers are rusted or missing. The deck was built without a permit and doesn’t meet current code. A deck built in the 1990s here is often at the end of its structural life even if the surface still looks fine. From the owner
We get calls every January from homeowners who want a kitchen done by March. Sometimes we can make it work. Often, we can't, and the reason is almost always cabinets. Most cabinet orders, even the more straightforward ones, run 8 to 14 weeks from the order date to delivery. Custom or semi-custom can push past that. By the time you add permitting, scheduling, and the actual install, a project that starts its planning in October can realistically be finished by late winter or early spring. A project that starts planning in December is a spring project at best, and that's if everything moves. We have project slots available right now for early 2027 starts in Shrewsbury and Worcester. If you want one of them, the time to get into an estimate is now, not after the holidays. If you're planning for next season, now's the time to talk. Send me a message and let's look at your timeline., Marcony Araujo and Romero Araujo, Founder

From the owner
A long-lasting tile floor starts with the prep work you’ll never see—here’s how proper plywood spacing, fastening, backerboard installation, and floor leveling help prevent cracks and create a better finished floor. Most people, and sadly contractors included, don’t know this: plywood must have gaps (expansion joints) in between pieces. Plywood moves horizontally quite a bit. Depending on moisture, it ranges from 3/32” to 7/32”. So the minimum plywood joint is required to be ⅛” on all sides to the adjacent sheets, and ¼” at the perimeter ( see ANSI 108.01 section 3.4). Below is an example from a job I’m currently on. Give me a rating for my boots bombing the photo. As far as securing the plywood, fasten every 6” at the edges and 12” in the field not on the joists. So the second layer of plywood after the subfloor is more like a slip coupler instead of another sub floor layer. Disconnecting it directly from the floor joists keeps it from moving as much with the tongue and groove sub floors’ movement, but that still isn’t enough for tile. After that, if you’re going to install a backerboard variation (foam, cement, hardie, etc) then spreading the mortar on the plywood requires that the gaps not be filled in with mortar. Also note that with either ¼” or ½” backerboard on the floor, the minimum 1 ¼” collated screws will completely penetrate the entire layer of cement board, top plywood layer, and into the sub floor, further strengthening the floor setup.
